#200. US midterm elections 2026 live: Americans go to the polls to decide control of Congress

Voters are casting their ballots across the US in a referendum on Donald Trump’s agenda

What are the races to watch and why do they matter?

Midterm elections 2026: what time do the polls close today?

The US Congress has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate. Both must approve federal legislation before it can become law and both play important roles in overseeing the executive branch.

The House is elected every two years, meaning all 435 voting seats are contested at every congressional election. The Senate has 100 members serving staggered six-year terms, so roughly a third of its seats are up for election every two years.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives. Republicans are defending a narrow majority, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.

35 seats in the Senate. Thirty-three seats are up in regular elections, along with two special elections in Florida and Ohio to fill the remainder of terms that were vacated early. Republicans currently hold 53 seats, against 47 held by Democrats and independents who caucus with them. Democrats need to gain four seats to secure a majority.

39 governorships. Voters will choose governors in 36 states and three US territories.

Thousands of state legislative seats, as well as local offices, judicial contests and ballot measures on issues including taxes, abortion rights and voting rules.

The elections for Congress will determine which party controls Congress for the final two years of Trump’s second term. The governorships and state legislative contests will shape policymaking closer to home, from education and reproductive rights to taxation and the administration of elections.

The midterms have a long history of punishing the occupant of the White House. The president’s party has lost House seats in 18 of the past 20 midterm elections, a 90% rate of loss that stretches back to 1946.

The first election results of the 2026 midterms have come in from Guam, the Pacific island territory across the International Date Line where America’s day – and its elections – officially begin.

The unofficial results published by the Guam Election Commission show that Republicans wrested away control of Guam’s governorship, with the GOP ticket headed by Vicente Ada. Democrats, meanwhile, flipped the state’s nonvoting delegate to Congress blue, as voters opted to send Democratic candidate Alicia Anne Garrido Limtiaco to Washington.

Donald Trump took to his personal social media platform to remark on the results, which he considered a strong showing for the Republicans.

“Guam, which has always been considered strongly Democrat, just had an early call for a REPUBLICAN Victory in the top spot, Governor — Congratulations to Tony Ada! Also, the Republicans have the Majority in the State Senate. Wow, hopefully that’s an indication for things to come!”

Voters in Minneapolis have slowly been trickling in to vote at a polling site in a predominantly immigrant community, as groups and organizations observe at various sites around the city.

Observers and voters have told the Guardian it has been a relatively relaxed election day so far at the site, likely due to a strong early voting push in the state.

As voters arrive to the community center in downtown Minneapolis, a reverend has been standing in front to observe, in case of any anxieties or escalations and to make sure people can exercise their right to vote.

Reverend Shandon Klein, a progressive pastor from the Park Avenue United Methodist Church in Minneapolis said she is “keeping a watchful eye over the polling place just to make sure I’m a non-anxious presence that’s available here and just ensuring that everybody has access to voting.”

Klein told the Guardian that various community groups are visiting polling sites around the city to support for voters.

“There’s a general just feeling of empowerment and really excited to get out there and vote,” Klein said.

The voters in the primarily Somali neighborhood have been arriving to the community center in downtown Minneapolis. So far, no federal law enforcement officials have been spotted, despite threats by the Trump administrating of deploying them to voting sites.

At the end of 2025 and early this year, Minnesota became a major target for the Trump administration. Federal immigration officials descended on the area in a large-scale operation. Community groups organized rapid response teams throughout the city to prevent officials from arresting immigrants. The immigration operation led to the shooting deaths of two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

Many groups involved in the immigration rapid response work have shifted their attention onto the elections.

Earlier, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton spoke after voting in the midterm election that will decide the Ohio governor’s race. Acton called her opponent a “danger” and added that she believed he had “crossed the line” during their campaigns. In the closing weeks of the contest, Ramaswamy aired a controversial ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother that prompted bipartisan backlash across the country.

Erin Moynihan, an Iowa Democrat, knocks doors in a working-class neighborhood in south Des Moines, finding waterlogged campaign literature on the doorsteps of several homes already visited by Iowa candidates.

At one door, she asks a man if he was planning to vote today. “Already did,” he responded. Most people aren’t home, or aren’t answering their doors. One man asks if she’s selling stuff.

And then she meets Jerry Heck, a 92-year-old who said he’s voted in nearly all elections in his life. He said he doesn’t plan to go out and vote today. He didn’t get his mail ballot in time, and several health conditions prevent him from going in person. Moynihan offers to find him a ride and get him there, but he’s not interested.

“Everybody that votes, I appreciate them, and I should have done it, but I’m not going to,” he said.

Heck is no fan of Donald Trump, and he closely follows politics. He likes Rob Sand, the democratic candidate for governor. But he says he’s “disgusted” with the whole political process at this point.

“I don’t know how you people cope with it who are younger than me,” Heck said. “It’s just total insanity nowadays.”

Moynihan said she will keep working today to find a way for Heck to get to the polls.

David Boy, an attorney from Johns Creek, Georgia voted for Republicans down the ballot on Tuesday, despite his antipathy toward Donald Trump.

“I don’t like Trump. I’ve never voted for him,” Boy said. “I want to go to my deathbed saying I never did.”

Boy said he wants the war in Iran to end, and gas prices to go down and for Congress to set aside partisan politics and accomplish something useful.

He told the Guardian: “I’ve got school-age kids, so making sure the schools are good for them. Taxes. I’m in the prime earning years right now so paying taxes … and then also for me, personally, my faith and integrity and moral issues. And then, I want things to be run well. Honestly, I want our government to be run efficiently and effectively.”

double quotation markI like how Jackson has sort of distanced himself from Trump and has been saying ‘hey, I’m willing to work with both sides.’ I’m hoping he won’t be another one of these politicians who is just a pawn of Trump and does what Trump says. Hopefully he stays an outsider.

Meanwhile, from behind a groovy pair of hitman glasses, Jennifer Thurman, a market researcher in Suwanee, had one eye out for malcontents at a voting station at Suwanee’s recreation center on Tuesday.

Amid the reported presence of federal elections observers in and around Atlanta has inspired a concomitant degree of vigilance, she said she was prepared to “face off against anybody who tried to stop someone else from voting.”

Thurman, who has always been a Democrat, voted a straight Democratic ballot. Abortion rights drew her to Democratic politics, she said, adding: “It’s not just about women. It is about whether the government can tell someone what to do with their body, which seems to me to be the most personal thing — more personal than voting.”

The effects of “haphazard, slapdash” Doge cuts on foreign aid, the deterioration of our international relationships and the damage to the fundamental functioning of the government has left scars that may take a long time to heal, Thurman said, adding that she expects the next two years to be frustrating.

double quotation markI think [Trump is] going to try everything. He’s so morally reprehensible. And when he says he can grab anything he wants, that’s what he’s doing. Somebody who does sexual assault will take what he wants, and that’s him.

If Democrats take the House and Senate, “we’ll be able to at least stop the worst, and investigate,” she said, “but they need a policy platform to run on in ’28 and this is their time to develop it.”

Thurman added that she wants congressional Democrats to offer the best legislation they can and to be “caught trying” - even if it doesn’t pass. “And then they need to publicize what they try to do … so that they can be seen, because so often what happens legislatively gets sort of buried.”

Voter turnout has surged in the lead up to this year’s midterm election, with the number of early ballots cast significantly outstripping the totals from the 2022 midterm.

Elections workers across the country were expecting that trend to continued into election day. Officials in states including North Carolina, Georgia, and Michigan — a major battleground – reported strong turnout in the opening hours of voting.

One Dearborn voter who cast a full Republican ballot on Tuesday said she wishes the race for governor were getting more attention, because she believes Michigan is falling behind.

“Michigan is in a dumpster fire,” said Sona, a resident in her 60s who didn’t want to give her last name.

She described herself as a lifelong conservative who opposes abortion and is concerned about “transgenderism”, specifically transgender athletes in women’s sports. She also pointed to wages she said run about $10,000 below those in neighboring states, and to high electric bills.

Democrat Jocelyn Benson is running for governor, and Sona said she expects her to win despite what she sees as a weak campaign.

“Benson has hardly put up a fight for anything, and yet she’s gonna probably skate right in there,” she said. “I just don’t understand it.”

Meanwhile, Ali Bakri, a 33-year-old small business owner and Dearborn native, said that he is voting for Abdul El-Sayed for US Senate because he sees him as a champion of small businesses and everyday people.

“He advocates for the small guys more than the big guys,” Bakri, who owns his own coffee shop, said.

Bakri said he has met El-Sayed more than a dozen times, attended some of his campaign events, and has been a booster of his ever since El-Sayed ran for governor in 2018.

Bakri explained how it matters to him to get as many people from his community into positions of power as possible, and he described El-Sayed as “more of a community man.”

double quotation markThe big guys have enough support. We need our voices to be heard on the small side. And that’s what I respect.

In an interview with the Guardian in Topeka, Adam Hamilton, who wore a pin with the bible verse, “love one another,” said that he believes that many people watching the election abroad may “know Americans are good people,” but are “really uncertain about our government right now.”

He described his campaign as an effort to “stand up to the bully that’s Washington DC right now, doing things that are not okay.”

“We have been in an uncertain time, and I think we are restoring America to who it is,” he said. “We want our trading partners and our allies to know that you can count on America.”

This year’s midterms have largely revolved around the issue of affordability, and Hamilton said his first priority to get costs lower for Kansans would be to end the war in Iran, which have nearly doubled diesel and fertilizer prices for the thousands of farmers in the state. Kansas’s land is about 88% farmland, and roughly 1 in 5 of its residents work in the agriculture industry, according to the state’s department of agriculture.

If Hamilton wins tonight, it would be the first time since 1938 - in 94 years - that a Democrat would occupy a Kansas senate seat. Polls show him effectively tied with his Republican opponent, Roy Marshall, a competitiveness Hamilton credits to desire for decency among people in his state.

“Kansans are just salt of the earth, decent people. They want to do the right thing … and their senator, who I’m running against, is not speaking up for them,” he said. “And I think they wish that somebody had the courage to speak up to their boss and say this is not okay.”

After all the brouhaha over the two Dan Sullivans, after all Donald Trump’s legal threats and talk of blocking certification of the vote, Anchorage finally got to have its say on Tuesday from the far-flung vastness of Alaska.

With the sun not yet risen over the snowcapped Chugach mountains that surround the city, voters descended on the city’s Midtown Mall from 7am in a critical US Senate race that could determine which party controls the upper chamber.

One of the first to arrive, still in pitch blackness, was a former mayor of Anchorage and a candidate in Alaska’s gubernatorial race, David Bronson, who had some stern words for anyone considering voting Democrat in this highly-charged election.

“You only need to look as far as Great Britain and France to see what happens when you vote left,” the Republican said. “You get unrestricted immigration.”

Asked about the war with Iran that Trump started, he said: “It’s not really a war, it’s more of a policing action.”

John House, 62, a carpenter living and working Anchorage, had a similarly sharp warning for fellow voters amid polls which show the Democratic senate candidate Mary Peltola with a slim lead over the Republican incumbent senator Dan Sullivan.

“You’d be a damn fool to vote Democrat, we’ll go backwards,” he said. “You can’t give free medicaid to everybody. The trans stuff - they would drag this country down.”

Was he still backing Trump? “He talks too much but he’s done so much for us. No tax on overtime - that means a lot to me.”

The furor over the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the ballot appeared not to unduly concern Tuesday’s voters. After the New York Times (paywall) reported that Democratic operatives aligned with Peltola had recruited a second Dan Sullivan to run as a ballot-stacking ruse, all hell broke loose.

Peltola has denied the allegations. But they inflamed Trump’s attempt to interfere in the race, with the justice department launching a lawsuit that has since been dismissed, and the current governor of Alaska initiating a criminal investigation.

Juanita Cupa, 30, turning up at the Midtown Mall polling station, was entirely unfazed. “It’s just been a lot of foolishness around this, on both sides. We’re all ready for it to be over,” she said with a weary shrug.

Cupa voted for Peltola, driven by two motivating factors. The first is her animus towards Trump. “He is spreading hatred, racism. His leadership is disgusting - the way he talks about women and human life.”

The second factor was more personal. Prices are up, and life is tough. She spends $120 every two weeks filling up her truck which she can’t do without in Alaska’s snowy wilderness.

She is so hard up that she has had to move back in with her parents. “I’m living check to check.”

Chaunice Carr, 27, also voted for Peltola. She said that turning up on election day and casting her ballot was “insanely important” to her.

Asked why, she replied: “There are a lot of bad things happening in Alaska, in the world. A lot of violence. ICE raids, people being deported in horrid ways. I’m hoping that today we can start to get that violence out of our lives.”

A steady stream of voters entered the Merrill auditorium polling station in Portland’s busy downtown district in mid-morning, leading to queues of up to half an hour to cast a ballot, according to organizers.

Of six voters interviewed by the Guardian, five said they had voted Democrat, favoring the party’s candidate Troy Jackson over the five-term GOP incumbent, Susan Collins, in the race for US Senate.

All of those asked cited national issues associated with Donald Trump’s second presidency as motivating their vote. All the Democrat voters interviewed cited issues relating to democracy, human rights and Trump’s perceived authoritarianism before economic issues.

Maple Razsa, 55, a global studies professor at Colby College in Waterville, said he had motivated by the Trump administration’s support for Israel’s actions in Gaza, which he termed a genocide.

But he also feared growing authoritarianism at home. He been teaching a class on the 1973 coup that overthrew the leftist Chilean president Salvador Allende, ushering in a military dictatorship, and saw parallels with the contemporary US, citing the increasing attacks by Immigration, Customs and Enforcement (ICE) agents on American citizens.

double quotation markI’m concerned about ICE raids that have been happening here in Portland. The political system is just run amok at this point.

One of the [preparations] for the military coup in Chile was that the military was sent out on raids before it happened to get it used to targeting its own populations, so that it was ready for the coup. It’s very hard for me not to see that with the targeting of my neighbors here.

Todd Cox, 63, a technology professional, said he voted for Jackson despite have twice previously voted for Collins because of “concern for the direction the country is going in”.

double quotation markWe definitely haven’t become kinder and gentler under this administration. There’s a lot of bullying that goes on. It goes back to affordability - it’s the war in Iran, that shouldn’t be happening. It’s the disregard for the rule of law. It just seems like they’re thumbing their nose at it.

Amal Kareem, 48, had emigrated to the US in 2009 from Iraq, where he had been an interpreter for American military occupation forces.

His vote for Jackson had been driven by concern over rising Islamophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment, as well as issues arising from the Iran war. The economic impact of rising fuel costs meant he had to work two jobs to make ends meet.

double quotation markA lot of Americans are being badly influenced by the news coverage, especially on Fox. This gives them a false idea of why people move to this country, without even having talked to them or their background.

But if our countries were stable and didn’t have war, we would never have thought of leaving our homeland. Now we have another war, and its impacting everyone. The president broke the promises he made before coming to office, when he said he wouldn’t be fighting any other war.

Sandra Braden, 85, said she had voted Democrat because of the administration’s “cruelty and greed”.

double quotation markIt makes me feel so ashamed and sad.

Diane Clukey-Chenard, 59, said she had been inspired to vote against Collins because of a concern for LGBTQ and transgender rights and by the senator’s 2018 vote to confirm the conservative US supreme court justice, Brett Kavanaugh, who subsequently voted in favor of a ruling overturning the national right to abortion.

double quotation markMy concerns are economic and also women’s rights. I just hope we can finally start supporting our LGBTQ+ community, especially trans folks, and that we can also get universal health care.

One 63-year-man who said he had voted Collins declined to give his name, saying: “This town doxxes you if they don’t like how you voted.”

He added: “I voted straight Republican. I don’t know much about the issues, but I’m not ready to throw away Israel yet. I don’t really see the war in Iran as a real war. What have we lost? Dozens. We lose hundreds and thousands in these war and if they have a nuclear bomb, we’re going to have a nuclear war anyway.

“If we didn’t go in, [Benjamin] Netanyahu [Israel’s prime minister] was going to take them out, so we’d have been in a world war.”

Ron DeSantis isn’t on the ballot on Tuesday as Florida voters decide who will succeed the termed-out Republican governor. But he still managed to raise eyebrows with comments about his plans for the 2028 presidential race.

DeSantis, despite being hyped as a rising young Republican star, flamed out miserably in his campaign for his party’s 2024 nomination, which Donald Trump won. It was widely assumed that, once he completes his second and final term as Florida governor in January, he would turn his attention to a new White House run in 2028.

He appeared to cast doubt on that eventuality in an interview on Tuesday with political commentator Stephen A Smith on his SiriusXM show Straight Shooter with Stephen A.

double quotation markWe’ll see what happens. Maybe someday. I don’t know about ‘28, maybe later, maybe.

Smith pressed him further on his plans after leaving office. DeSantis joked: “Old governors never die, they just fade away, right? So we’ll see what happens.”

DeSantis has always enjoyed something of a fractious relationship with Trump, and expressed more criticism of the president when Smith asked him about the war in Iran.

“He obviously ran saying he wasn’t going to do a Middle East war. They did. So we have some of our voters who’ve checked out because they’re like, ‘I didn’t want any more Middle East wars, and now we’re doing it’,” DeSantis said. He went on:

double quotation markGas is higher. It hurts people, working-class people, and it’s higher because of this conflict. That’s just a fact. If you can’t admit that to voters, then you’re gaslighting them, and they’re not going to listen to you on other things.

If [the war] drags on for the rest of his presidency, it’s going to be devastating to his ability to get anything done, and it is going to be very, very difficult for Republicans.

DeSantis endorsed Republican congressman Byron Donalds to become Florida’s next governor in a close race with Democrat David Jolly.

#198. Yemen: Houthi clashes near Taiz leave residents in a 'state of panic'

Fighting between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Yemeni government forces has intensified around the city of Taiz. Residents face growing shortages of food, water and medical supplies as thousands flee their homes.

Four months into the fighting in Yemen between the Iran-backed Houthi movement and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, clashes are concentrated around Taiz in the country's southwest. Yemeni authorities have warned civilians of sniper fire from surrounding hillsides. Houthi forces have also largely blocked the delivery of goods to Taiz, which is under the control of government forces.

Taiz is Yemen's third-largest city, with a population of around 1 million people. However, fighting has displaced around 134,000 people in the Taiz governorate region, accordingto the International Organization for Migration. The governorate accounts for almost half of the more than 319,000 people displaced across western Yemen, the organization said on November 1, 2026.

"The Houthis have blocked fuel, water and medical supplies, basically all things required for hospitals to function properly," Niku Jafarnia, Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, told DW. "Even those who can reach hospitals may not be receiving the care they need," she said, adding that it has had a devastating impact on people's health, particularly those with chronic illnesses.

Ammar, a 45-year-old photographer in Taiz, told DW on Monday that he sees people in a "state of panic" and yet he feels that "the determination not to submit to the Houthis is very strong."

Afnan, the mother of a schoolchild in Taiz, told DW that "neighbors share the little food they have and help each other and many people in Taiz refuse to flee." She and the other residents who spoke to DW asked that their full names not be published, fearing reprisals.

Hanan, a 30-year-old mother of three, said that prices have skyrocketed while there is almost no petrol, cooking gas or drinking water left in the city. "This increases the mental load on people who are already scared by hearing the clashes of the fighting day and night," she said. Despite this, she numbers among those who have decided to stay.

Meanwhile, Nabil Shamsan, the governor of Taiz, told DW that negotiations are underway to bring food, fuel and water back to the city. While it remains to be seen when and under what conditions this might happen, international aid organizations remain extremely concerned.

"Fighting and insecurity around Taiz is making it unsafe for civilians to move freely and also for our staff to deliver aid," said Alison Bottomley, an advocacy adviser with the Norwegian Refugee Council in Yemen. "This is preventing us from reaching the 7,000 people we are supporting with emergency tents, blankets and educational activities for displaced children," she told DW, calling on both factions to allow "civilians and humanitarian workers to move safely."

During the previous Yemen conflict, which began in 2014 and largely ended with a UN-brokered truce in 2022, Ansar Allah, the formal name of the Houthi group, had already laid siege to Taiz in 2015 and 2016. That siege brought the population close to famine and caused a humanitarian crisis, but the Houthis never captured the city.

In turn, Taiz, as a bastion of resistance, represents something the Houthis have struggled to subdue for more than a decade, Hisham Al-Omeisy, a senior Yemeni adviser with UK-based advisory firm Coral Core Consultants, told DW. "The city symbolizes a deeply rooted tradition of political pluralism, civic resistance and rejection of the Houthi model of rule," he said, adding that the city's continued resistance is both a military obstacle and a political challenge to the Houthis' claim that their authority across Yemen is inevitable.

Following the truce in 2022, the Houthis controlled the capital Sanaa, most of northern Yemen and parts of the center, while the internationally recognized government controlled much of the west and the south including the city of Aden. However, fighting reignited in late July and the clashes intensified in September, as the Houthis seized territory from forces loyal to the internationally recognized government.

Control of the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, is contested. The precise territorial situation remains unclear, while the Houthis retain the capacity to threaten maritime traffic. The conflict continues to escalate, alongside an exchange of missile and drone attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

Data on the number of people injured or killed in Yemen varies because of the ongoing fighting and separate statistics given by the Houthi movement and the government's health authorities. According to the latest WHO Health Cluster situation report, at least 1,677 people had been killed and 7,395 injured as of October 25, 2026.

Meanwhile, seizing Taiz is highlighted as a key strategic step by analysts. "Taiz would give the Houthis a major advantage in consolidating their hold over northern Yemen while opening the way for further expansion toward the south and the Red Sea coast," Al-Omeisy said, adding that controlling Taiz would give them stronger cards in any future negotiations.

"Taiz is far more than simply another military front for the Houthis," he noted.

"However, the Houthis may not actually need to capture Taiz to achieve many of their objectives," Hisham Al-Omeisy said. "If they can isolate the city, sever its remaining supply lines and neutralize it as a military threat, they could consolidate their positions along the western coast while tying down significant government forces," he added.

"My greater concern is that the Houthis could use gains around Taiz to progressively weaken and fragment the anti-Houthi camp, rather than immediately launch a full-scale offensive against Aden," Al-Omeisy told DW, adding that the Houthis have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to exploit divisions among their opponents, and those divisions remain one of the government's greatest vulnerabilities.

#195. Man who drugged and raped wife found many men ‘whose fantasy is an unconscious woman’, court told

Nine men stand trial in Manchester accused of participating in abuse at couple’s home in Stockport, or encouraging it online

The Stockport man who drugged, raped and sexually assaulted his wife personally found a large number of the “many, many men whose fantasy is an unconscious and unresponsive woman”, a court has heard.

Nine men are on trial at Manchester Minshull Street crown court, accused of either participating in the abuse, which took place at the couple’s home, or encouraging it online.

The husband, who is in his 60s, has pleaded guilty to multiple offences against his wife, committed over a period of more than 20 years. He cannot be named in order to protect the anonymity of his victim.

On the second day of the prosecution case, Louise Oakley KC told the jury the husband had met the first defendant, Robert Stewart, 70, who also lived in Stockport, Greater Manchester, on Craigslist in 2015.

His interaction with Stewart, the jury was told, was “to be his blueprint for future offending”. Stewart had asked if the victim would ever participate in a “threesome”, but the husband “made it clear that there was absolutely no chance of that”, the court heard.

The two men then discussed the use of date rape drugs and opportunities to spike her drink to try to render the woman unconscious. Stewart provided the husband with antidepressants and Tramadol, a strong painkiller, on agreement the husband would invite Stewart to go to their home if she was unconscious, the jury was told.

The contact between the two men was, Oakley said, “no doubt the first big step [the husband] took in realising his own fantasy of having another man come to him and ‘fuck’ his unaware wife.”

The court heard the husband had visited news websites and online forums, where he searched for information on date rape drugs, GHB and sleeping tablets. “[The husband’s] perversity did not wane,” Oakley told the court. “He wanted to share her but recognised that alcohol alone was not going to be enough.

“So desperate, you may think, was he, he would share imagery of [his wife] with complete strangers and then discuss how they would supply him with drugs in order that she be raped. Sharing her, his desire, in their own home.”

The court heard that the husband had also discussed with a second defendant, David Graves, 60, from Ilkeston in Derbyshire, the need to find “something to knock her out completely”.

Graves, described as a “non-contact offender”, had supplied the husband with tablets to drug his wife, and in return the husband agreed to send him imagery of the abuse.

The husband had asked Graves to post the tablets to the house of a close relative of his wife’s who had recently died, the court heard. “The house where [the relative] had been living was empty,” Oakley told the court. “Does it get any worse than that?”

The court heard Graves then became “incredibly impatient” when there was a delay in sending the images. The husband told him “he tried the tablets but they tasted so bitter and his wife thought there was something wrong with the curry,” Oakley said. “Obviously the tablets he had put in the food.”

A third defendant, Philip Wild, 58, from Stockport, had visited the couple’s home in August 2023, the court heard. The husband told him he had to be quiet, so he didn’t wake the victim, and advised him to step out on to the landing if she stirred, and that “he would deal with the situation”.

Wild had touched the woman sexually, and “was fully aware that [she] was not conscious and not able to consent to any sexual activity”, Oakley told the court.

The husband put Wild, a taxi driver, in touch with another man, Graham Brougham, who also lived close to the couple’s Stockport address, the court heard, and they discussed having sex with the woman using WhatsApp.

The name of the WhatsApp group was originally a pseudonym for the woman that her husband had used online, but was later renamed to “Taxi” in an apparent bid to avoid suspicion.

The jury was told the husband also sent pictures of his wife to another “non-contact offender”, Daniel Rayner, 42, from Whitstable in Kent.

Rayner repeatedly asked the husband for images, Oakley said, and “he knows that what he wants, he gets.”

The pair also discussed drugging the victim, and Rayner’s ability to obtain the date rape drug GHB. “[Rayner] knew [the wife] was unaware, and he knew that she was being sexually abused by her husband,” Oakley said.

Five other men are on trial accused of participating in the abuse of the woman. They are Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester; Alan Keelan, 42, from Manchester; Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport; Mohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abode; and Richard Townsend, 37, from Heywood in Greater Manchester. All of the men on trial deny the charges against them.

Three men – Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport; Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee; and Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich in Cheshire – have already admitted to abusing the woman, while Karl Lindsay, 56, from Somerset, has pleaded guilty to “non-contact” offences.

“The sad reality of this case is that there are many, many men whose fantasy is an unconscious and unresponsive woman,” Oakley told the court. “[The husband] found a large number of them. We suggest they sit in this dock today.”

While all of the men may not know exactly what drugs the husband had administered, Oakley said, “they expected her to be ‘wasted’ and ‘out of it.’

“The harsh reality is,” Oakley said, “any right-minded human being who walked into that room, that bedroom, with two eyes, two ears, and half a brain would have realised she was not conscious.”

“They knew. It’s what they wanted,” she added. “Anyone who didn’t, would have run a country mile.”

While the defendants may claim the wife had consented, Oakley said, “any defendant that suggests they had any conversation with her, I suggest is lying.”

The trial, which is expected to last for three months, continues.

The interior ministry estimated that 320,000 people had demonstrated nationwide, a smaller number than the previous two Saturdays. The police and protesters clashed in Paris and other cities.

Hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets in cities across France again on Saturday, the latest expression of national grievance that has led to clashes between protesters and the police and kept the country on edge.

As dusk fell and official rallies wound down, unauthorized marches splintered off in Paris, stoking fresh fears of chaos as night approached.

Adding to those fears: Halloween, which falls on Saturday. The French authorities, citing calls on social media for people to revolt that encouraged them to wear masks and costumes, warned that the risk of a new outbreak of violence was high.

In Paris, tensions began flaring between protesters and the police in the late afternoon, as officers fired tear gas at people who refused to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration, compared with 110,000 last Saturday. After the main demonstration ended, hundreds of protesters, many masked and clad in black, formed an unauthorized procession in eastern Paris.

The interior ministry estimated that nationwide, 320,000 people demonstrated, compared with 410,000 last week. Protesters and the police also clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes.

Corentin Schnell, a 19-year-old engineering student, took part in the unauthorized march in Paris because, he said, he was angered by accounts of the police using tear gas and stun grenades against protesters in past weeks. “I’ve come to demonstrate and to try to provide medical care — to limit the damage, regardless of which side it’s on,” he said.

Earlier in the week, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, promised to deploy 70,000 police officers, matching the numbers on Oct. 24. That operation helped keep a lid on outbreaks of arson and looting, although then, too, there were clashes as the police tried to disperse the crowds in the evening.

There was ample fuel for a repeat of those combustible scenes. Students, who are returning to school on Monday after a two-week break, were not mollified by the government’s initial response to their demands. The Education Ministry agreed to cap some class sizes, offer low-interest loans to rebuild school buildings and phase out an unpopular online college admissions platform.

The students vowed to go on protesting. Their two-month-old movement has grown to include university students, public workers and veterans of the “yellow vest” movement that convulsed France from 2018 to 2020.

The authorities have said they are most worried about trouble breaking out after nightfall.

“We are seeing numerous calls to gather coming from the far left, the radicalized extreme left, and from certain radicalized ‘yellow vests’ websites, which are urging people to attend rallies or public gatherings starting at 8 p.m. in many cities across France,” Mr. Nuñez said at a news conference.

Some of the messages were violent, Mr. Nuñez said, calling for “revolution” and “insurrection.” Those gatherings will be forbidden, and any attempt to gather despite the ban will lead to arrests, he said.

Demonstrators have been encouraged on social media to turn up wearing Halloween costumes. Mr. Nuñez warned that it was a criminal offense to conceal one’s face during a demonstration that disrupted public order.

Social media: French officials are increasingly concerned about social media’s role in attracting people and inciting violent behavior. Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself. Read more ›

Far-right activists: While the government has blamed far-left activists for much of the mayhem, officials confirmed that bands of young men with links to the far right have also infiltrated the demonstrations. They use the pretext of protecting shop owners but often clash with far-left groups.

Widening movement: The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month. Read more ›

The authorized demonstration in Paris has come to an end, with some clashes with the police. In its place, a spontaneous procession of several hundred protesters took shape along Avenue Daumesnil in eastern Paris. Many were dressed in black and had their faces covered. Part of the crowd was singing and dancing to songs blasted on speakers. As the crowd got closer to a square with bars and restaurants full of customers, some waiters hurried to close outdoor seating areas as police officers arrived on motorcycles. Even with the heavy police presence, no clashes erupted and the protesters marched into the night.

Among the protesters in the unauthorized demonstration were Morgane Voisin, 22, and Corentin Schnell, 19, both of whom were wearing white outfits indicating that they were “street medics,” or those able to deliver first aid. Ms. Voisin, a sales consultant, said she came to demonstrate because her younger siblings had faced harsh conditions in high school. Mr. Schnell, an engineering student, said he was prompted to join when his little brother told him about getting tear-gassed and almost hit by a stun grenade at a protest earlier this month. “The mere fact that people are being injured by the police makes me furious,” Mr. Schnell said. “So I’ve come to demonstrate and to try to provide medical care — to limit the damage, regardless of which side it’s on.” On Saturday, the pair said they saw one person who had been injured in the head, but aid arrived quickly. “Long live youth!” Ms. Voisin said.

I can hear loud bangs at the end of the demonstration route and I can see many people running backward, as well as tear gas in the distance. Some protesters are throwing mortar-like fireworks.

The mood at the Paris protest has definitely changed. Though I can still hear some protesters singing, the protest has turned violent.

Police officers are now blocking many of the roads in the neighborhood at the end of the demonstration route. I saw a young woman surrounded by medics — she was bleeding from the face. I saw flames at the end of one avenue. I also saw police officers charge toward the crowd. Some residents are trying to make their way back home quickly, covering their faces to avoid tear gas.

Tensions in Paris continue to rise. Police are skirmishing with 200 to 300 rioters who have refused to disperse at the end of a rally. The Paris police said the rioters threw Molotov cocktails and fireworks at officers. A car was set afire.

Tensions are now flaring between protesters and the police in Paris. Police are firing rounds of tear gas at people, who are refusing to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration, compared with 110,000 last Saturday.

The Interior Ministry estimated that 320,000 people took part in protests across the country today. That is somewhat fewer than last week (410,000) and the week before (550,000).

The demonstration in Paris remains peaceful, even festive. But police and protesters have clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes. Tear gas and water cannons have been deployed as the police try to disperse crowds. Violence typically breaks out at the end of these rallies, when people refuse to leave the scene.

I am walking along the authorized route for the demonstration in Paris. For the most part, the mood has been festive. Someone even dropped candy from his balcony, drawing cheers from the crowd.

After, I watched a half-dozen protesters dressed in black and wearing masks push trash bins in the middle of the crowd. One was already burning as they made their way, and they set the second on fire not far from where a police unit was stationed. Other demonstrators used water to put out the fire, causing a small clash with the ones wearing in black. “That’s no way to protest,” one of the demonstrators who put out the fire said.

The protest in Paris has a joyous and playful atmosphere. Brass bands are playing music, and many protesters have come dressed in Halloween costumes. Many said they wanted to help reverse the narrative set on Oct. 17 when riots spilled out of marches across France, leading to destruction and looting.

“I’m really worried about how the riots have been instrumentalized by the far right,” said Helen Olive, 50, who was among a group of parents who came dressed as “super parents.” “We want to turn that narrative around.”

Literature student Arthur Fleury, 20, arrived as a prisoner riding a dinosaur and wore a mask of the far-right politician Marine Le Pen. “Protests are about making demands but also having fun,” he said. “I was going for an absurd costume to capture the spirit of the movement.”

Early estimates from the French interior ministry suggest crowds are smaller today than the past two Saturdays. At 2 p.m., the ministry estimated that 15,000 people were taking part in 65 protests. That compares to 37,000 people last week at that time and 67,000 on Oct. 17. These numbers can be expected to grow as the day progresses. The ministry said it had arrested 27 people, compared with 217 by this time last Saturday. Protest organizers have yet to issue a crowd estimate; their numbers are typically far higher.

I’m at the Place de la Bastille. It is normally a bustling square, particularly on a beautiful, sunny Saturday. Now, police officers with shields and helmets patrol in groups. A loudspeaker blares a warning that gatherings and protests are forbidden to take place here by a police decree and that anyone who breaks it will be fined 135 euros.

Union and student organizers had again hoped to start their march here today, and again it was denied by the police and moved to the eastern edge of the city.

As France prepares for another round of protests, officials have grown increasingly concerned about the role played by social media in attracting people to demonstrations and inciting them to violent behavior.

Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself.

But in an interview on YouTube, Mr. Macron said that social media platforms would be required “to remove illegal content, and to be very vigilant about the use of certain features to prevent them from being misused by people who want to engage in looting or other such activities.”

That followed a report by a left-leaning online news site that Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had sent a letter to leading telecommunications operators, asking them to be prepared to block Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram. Mr. Lecornu’s office declined to comment on the authenticity of the letter.

Of the four reported recipients, one did not respond to questions and two declined to comment. A spokesman for the fourth, Orange, the only one in which the state is a shareholder, declined to confirm that a letter was received but said that “like any other operator, we are required to comply with the obligations legally imposed on us by the competent authorities, in accordance with applicable law.”

The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month.

Now, in cities across the country, antigovernment marchers are protesting expensive living conditions, high fuel prices and conditions in schools. Using the unrest as a smoke screen for vandalism, rioters and looters have also joined in.

With the protests in their second month, the police have arrested thousands, and politicians are divided over how to respond.

Here is a breakdown of what has happened.

Soon after returning from the summer break, students at a high school in the working class Parisian suburb of Créteil staged a protest, according to videos posted to social media on Sept. 18. The high schoolers objected to inadequate resources and high workloads.

Within days, students elsewhere around Paris initiated similar demonstrations. At schools in the capital’s poorest suburbs, students blocked entrances to protest crumbling infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms and what they say are flaws in the admissions system for higher education.

By Sept. 29, the unrest had spread to around 400 schools around the country, according to rally organizers.

The union of high school students said the blockades were a protest against a “lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classrooms.”

Students barricaded the entrances to some schools with obstacles including e-bikes, while others threw projectiles and set fire to trash cans.

The French education minister, Édouard Geffray, said that some of the students’ demands were “legitimate” but condemned the confrontational nature of their protests. He said that students had chased teachers and targeted school principals with firework-launching tubes.

By the end of September, nearly 80 people had been injured, and the authorities had detained more than 440, including many minors.

Within days, the number of schools engulfed in the protests had doubled. According to the Interior Ministry, by Oct. 2, they had spread to more than 1,000 schools across France, including 220 that were blockaded. University students also began taking part.

Around this time, the authorities said that the protests were mutating from legitimate expressions of educational grievances into something more dangerous, accusing people of shooting mortar-style fireworks, burning public buildings and looting.

By Oct. 2, nearly 400 police officers and over 230 school employees and students had been injured. The number of arrests climbed to 3,000.

The actions widened in October to encompass labor unions, parents and other activists, as different grievances converged into a mass protest.

On Oct. 6, around 256,000 people marched through Paris and 40 other French cities, according to the Interior Ministry. A union of high school students said protesters had occupied some 1,800 high schools.

The protests were mostly peaceful, but a fire was ignited in Lyon, and police officers used tear gas, including in Paris. The total number of arrested rose to 6,000, the authorities said. A major union of French judges and prosecutors and a human rights group accused the police of using disproportionate force, including against children as young as 14.

Two days later, on Oct. 8, smaller demonstrations were staged throughout the country, rallying around 71,500 people. The following week, the Interior Ministry said that 160,000 people joined marches on Oct. 13 across France.

More than half a million people joined 110 antigovernment marches throughout France on Oct. 17, according to an official estimate. A major union, the C.G.T., put the number even higher, at 800,000. Using either count, it was the largest day of protest since the demonstrations began in September.

Many of the marchers were peaceful, but some were not. Around the country, rioters vandalized around 1,500 shops, the authorities said. In Paris, where over 100,000 people marched peacefully, a few hundred rioters faced off against officers. According to the police, the rioters burned cars and smashed storefronts.

In the large town of Limoges, in central France, rioters set fire to the 19th-century City Hall. In a moment captured on video, the building’s spire collapsed in flames.

#192. HSBC's top execs face tense shareholders calling for a breakup

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on issues ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a plan to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank

Tucker said the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”

He said the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

“Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

Quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”

Pressed later by a shareholder on the issue, Quinn said a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

Investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, said she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who said he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out plans for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, said “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

The insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how quickly the deal came together.

“Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” said Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech

Quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

But he said he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

#190. UK makes huge aid cuts to Commonwealth nations despite warm words at Chogm summit

Nations in the group fare worse than others, with funding for nature projects especially hard hit even as climate crisis intensifies global need

The UK government has slashed overseas aid to Commonwealth countries, the Guardian can reveal, in contrast to the warm words for the group from King Charles and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, this week.

Amid sharp cuts in the UK’s aid budget overall, the Commonwealth has fared poorly, an analysis of the most recent and projected aid figures, seen by the Guardian, has shown.

Funding from the UK to the Commonwealth nations that previously had bilateral aid programmes will be cut from £546m in 2024-25 to £131m in 2028-29. Of that total, a large chunk – £68m – will go to Nigeria, leaving £63m for other countries.

The revelations come as the king attends the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) this week in Antigua, where he said it was “only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices” of slavery but where Burnham’s government fought to ensure that any discussion of reparations would be off the agenda.

The government has been cutting back on aid to countries that have been rapidly developing and are now judged to be middle income, such as India and Antigua, but the cuts to Commonwealth countries go much further, including many countries that are still among the poorest and many that are struggling under heavy debt burdens.

For example, Sierra Leone, one of the world’s least developed countries, will have its aid slashed from nearly £30m in 2024-25 to £5m in 2028-29. The UK and Sierra Leone will act as co-conveners of a strand of talks focusing on adaptation to the impacts of the climate crisis, at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey next week.

Aid to Rwanda, where the previous government had a scheme to send refugees, is also being cut from nearly £30m in 2024-25 to £5m in 2028-29. Aid to Tanzania will be slashed from £60m in 2025-26 to £5m in 2028-29. The Caribbean Development Team will have its funding cut from more than £98m in 2025-26 to £45m in 2026-27.

Nigeria will continue to represent one of the biggest destinations for Commonwealth aid, scheduled to receive £68m in 2028-29, down from £137m this year.

Funding for nature has been particularly hard-hit, experts told the Guardian, as many Commonwealth countries have not only had their aid funding slashed but have also been cut off from applying to the Darwin Initiative funds for nature protection. At least 26 countries from the Commonwealth have been prevented from receiving funds under the longstanding Darwin funding stream, worth about £40m a year.

Adrian Gahan, the UK lead at the Campaign for Nature charity, said: “UK aid to Commonwealth countries has fallen dramatically in recent years, with further cuts on the horizon. Some of the world’s most biodiversity-rich countries, many of which are also grappling with high levels of poverty, are facing severe reductions in support. For example, the UK’s Caribbean Development Team is set to see its funding cut by more than half between this year and next.”

He noted the contrast between the government’s stance at Chogm and the royal visit to the Caribbean. “This week, the king attended the launch of the Commonwealth nature initiative, a major new effort to protect nature across Commonwealth countries,” said Gahan. “Yet the UK government failed to make a financial contribution.”

Jean McLean, Oxfam GB chief influencing officer, said: “The UK government has really dropped the ball when it comes to the aid budget at exactly the moment when conflict, humanitarian crises, hunger and climate breakdown are driving global need to record levels. These cuts will not be felt in Westminster – they will be felt by families facing starvation, children denied healthcare and education, and communities struggling to survive the impacts of conflict and climate disasters.”

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office has been approached for comment. The Chogm meeting is set to wrap up on Wednesday.

Polish authorities said they carried out inspections of two passenger planes targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday but did not find any explosives, in a string of bomb threats that hit several European airports.

A bomb alert forced a LOT flight from London's Heathrow to make an unscheduled landing at Warsaw-Modlin airport, prompting the airport to shut down. Operations resumed around midday.

"The passengers were evacuated and the plane underwent security checks. Nothing was found," airport spokesman Adam Szablowski told the French AFP news agency. "The airport has been reopened and is operating normally."

A SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen also received a bomb threat before landing safely at Warsaw's central Chopin airport, where it underwent a security inspection.

No explosives were found on either plane. It was not immediately clear whether the threats were linked.

Also on Tuesday, a Ryanair flight from Manchester, UK, to Murcia, Spain, was hit by a bomb threat. It landed safely and underwent checks after all the passengers had disembarked.

The Spanish government's delegate in the region of Murcia, Francisco Lucas, confirmed on X that police "ruled out the presence of explosives on the plane."

"The International Airport of the Region of Murcia resumes its activity normally. Thanks to the emergency teams that have participated in the operation," he said.

And in the fourth such incident, the Reuters news agency reported that another flight traveling from Israel landed in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on Tuesday after a bomb threat was received via email. Counter-terrorism units were checking the plane for possible explosive devices, ​BTA news agency ⁠quoted Interior Minister Secretary General Lyubomir Nikolov as saying.

Later, two more bomb threats also targeted Ryanair flights from Lisbon and Dublin to Rome’s Fiumicino airport, according to Italian media. Air Force jets were deployed as a result. Both threats turned out to be false alarms.

The six threats on Tuesday come after a WizzAir flight from London to Sofia was redirected to the Hungarian capital, Budapest, on Monday after it received a bomb threat mid-air.

Similar such incidents have been reported across different European airports in recent weeks, with alerts later turning out to be false.

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, said it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the company. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

China Renaissance said in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance said auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company says

Trading in the company’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

Bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined company’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement said. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

#185. ‘Well-known individual’ fails in bid for injunction against Guardian and ITN

Person’s anonymity remains in place subject to any appeal against high court decision

A “well-known individual” has failed in his attempt to stop two media organisations from publishing allegations of inappropriate sexual activities towards young women, the high court has ruled.

The legal team for the anonymous individual, known in court only as PPT, had claimed he was “highly likely” to attempt suicide if the Guardian and ITN published the allegations, which he denies.

PPT’s legal team said he had attempted to kill himself twice since being contacted about the allegations in May. On the second occasion he absconded from a secure hospital to do so, they said.

The judge in the case, Mr Justice Nicklin, concluded he was satisfied that a decision to permit publication of the claims, the anticipation of publication and publication itself “would each materially increase the claimant’s risk of suicide”.

“That increase would be very substantial,” he said.

However, he found that it was for the state’s health services to protect PPT from harm in the form of mental health treatment, rather than the court’s responsibility to protect him by stopping the allegations from being published.

The claimant was seeking to block publication of the allegations by citing article two of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), which relates to the right to life; article three, relating to “inhuman or degrading treatment”; and article eight, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.

“The court has not assumed responsibility for the claimant’s psychiatric treatment or safety in the relevant sense,” Nicklin’s ruling states. “In the present case, the state has assumed responsibility for the claimant’s immediate safety through the psychiatric hospital and mental health services.

“The claimant is detained under the Mental Health Act 1983. The hospital exercises direct control over his care, observation, treatment, access to means of self-harm, leave and eventual discharge. It has assumed responsibility for the very risk with which article two is concerned.

“The evidence establishes that the hospital can provide significant protection. Inpatient treatment cannot eliminate the risk, but it materially reduces the likelihood of suicide.”

Nicklin said he had to balance the claimant’s rights with the media outlets’ right of freedom of expression.

The claimant had also made a claim under article eight of the ECHR about the impact his death, serious self-harm or a prolonged psychiatric admission would have upon his relationship with his son.

Nicklin said the claim had “very substantial weight”, but had to be balanced against the rights of the media companies to publish.

He said an injunction “would constitute an exceptionally serious interference” with their rights.

“It would prohibit the defendants from publishing the results of their investigations into allegations of serious wrongdoing by a prominent individual,” he found. “It would also prevent the sources whose accounts form part of those investigations from communicating their experiences to the public.”

The anonymity of the claimant remains in place because the judge granted him permission to appeal against the ruling.

Nicklin’s ruling stated that the Guardian and ITN allege that the claimant used his power and status as a well-known public figure to “establish contact with young women, who were also considerably younger than him, and engage, and/or seek to engage in inappropriate sexual activity”.

They claim the alleged incidents took place over several years and that some of them, if proved, could amount to criminal offences.

The judge emphasised that the current case did not examine whether the allegations against the claimant were true, but only whether the court should prevent the media outlets from publishing them.

He said the proposed journalism “did not lose its public interest value” merely because the allegations were disputed.

Nicklin also pointed to the implications of granting an injunction based on the risk of suicide.

“The principle contended for would apply whenever the court was satisfied that otherwise lawful publication would create a sufficiently grave risk of suicide or psychiatric harm and that restraint was the most effective means of preventing the trigger,” he found.

“The evidence does not identify a point at which publication would become safe merely through the passage of time. The relief sought would therefore be of uncertain and potentially indefinite duration.”

Nicklin rejected a proposal for the injunction to remain in place with a reassessment of the claimant’s condition after 18 months.

“The evidence does not … provide a clinical basis for selecting that or any other period for reassessment, or for concluding that treatment would by then have reduced the publication-related risk sufficiently,” he found.

#182. French officials eye social media’s role in promoting unrest.

The interior ministry estimated that 320,000 people had demonstrated nationwide, a smaller number than the previous two Saturdays. The police and protesters clashed in Paris and other cities.

Hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets in cities across France again on Saturday, the latest expression of national grievance that has led to clashes between protesters and the police and kept the country on edge.

As dusk fell and official rallies wound down, unauthorized marches splintered off in Paris, stoking fresh fears of chaos as night approached.

Adding to those fears: Halloween, which falls on Saturday. The French authorities, citing calls on social media for people to revolt that encouraged them to wear masks and costumes, warned that the risk of a new outbreak of violence was high.

In Paris, tensions began flaring between protesters and the police in the late afternoon, as officers fired tear gas at people who refused to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration, compared with 110,000 last Saturday. After the main demonstration ended, hundreds of protesters, many masked and clad in black, formed an unauthorized procession in eastern Paris.

The interior ministry estimated that nationwide, 320,000 people demonstrated, compared with 410,000 last week. Protesters and the police also clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes.

Corentin Schnell, a 19-year-old engineering student, took part in the unauthorized march in Paris because, he said, he was angered by accounts of the police using tear gas and stun grenades against protesters in past weeks. “I’ve come to demonstrate and to try to provide medical care — to limit the damage, regardless of which side it’s on,” he said.

Earlier in the week, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, promised to deploy 70,000 police officers, matching the numbers on Oct. 24. That operation helped keep a lid on outbreaks of arson and looting, although then, too, there were clashes as the police tried to disperse the crowds in the evening.

There was ample fuel for a repeat of those combustible scenes. Students, who are returning to school on Monday after a two-week break, were not mollified by the government’s initial response to their demands. The Education Ministry agreed to cap some class sizes, offer low-interest loans to rebuild school buildings and phase out an unpopular online college admissions platform.

The students vowed to go on protesting. Their two-month-old movement has grown to include university students, public workers and veterans of the “yellow vest” movement that convulsed France from 2018 to 2020.

The authorities have said they are most worried about trouble breaking out after nightfall.

“We are seeing numerous calls to gather coming from the far left, the radicalized extreme left, and from certain radicalized ‘yellow vests’ websites, which are urging people to attend rallies or public gatherings starting at 8 p.m. in many cities across France,” Mr. Nuñez said at a news conference.

Some of the messages were violent, Mr. Nuñez said, calling for “revolution” and “insurrection.” Those gatherings will be forbidden, and any attempt to gather despite the ban will lead to arrests, he said.

Demonstrators have been encouraged on social media to turn up wearing Halloween costumes. Mr. Nuñez warned that it was a criminal offense to conceal one’s face during a demonstration that disrupted public order.

Social media: French officials are increasingly concerned about social media’s role in attracting people and inciting violent behavior. Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself. Read more ›

The authorized demonstration in Paris has come to an end, with some clashes with the police. In its place, a spontaneous procession of several hundred protesters took shape along Avenue Daumesnil in eastern Paris. Many were dressed in black and had their faces covered. Part of the crowd was singing and dancing to songs blasted on speakers. As the crowd got closer to a square with bars and restaurants full of customers, some waiters hurried to close outdoor seating areas as police officers arrived on motorcycles. Even with the heavy police presence, no clashes erupted and the protesters marched into the night.

Among the protesters in the unauthorized demonstration were Morgane Voisin, 22, and Corentin Schnell, 19, both of whom were wearing white outfits indicating that they were “street medics,” or those able to deliver first aid. Ms. Voisin, a sales consultant, said she came to demonstrate because her younger siblings had faced harsh conditions in high school. Mr. Schnell, an engineering student, said he was prompted to join when his little brother told him about getting tear-gassed and almost hit by a stun grenade at a protest earlier this month. “The mere fact that people are being injured by the police makes me furious,” Mr. Schnell said. “So I’ve come to demonstrate and to try to provide medical care — to limit the damage, regardless of which side it’s on.” On Saturday, the pair said they saw one person who had been injured in the head, but aid arrived quickly. “Long live youth!” Ms. Voisin said.
